claim: C. elegans forms a memory of particular foods after experience and displays behavioral plasticity, increasing the feeding response when they subsequently recognize the familiar food.
source: Here, we show that the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans forms a memory of particular foods after experience and displays behavioral plasticity, increasing the feeding response when they subsequently recognize the familiar food.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1-3 showing differential feeding rates on familiar vs novel bacteria, and by the experimental design demonstrating memory retention over time intervals.

claim: Recognition of familiar food activates the pair of ADF chemosensory neurons.
source: We found that recognition of familiar food activates the pair of ADF chemosensory neurons, which subsequently increase serotonin release.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 12 showing ADF activation in response to familiar bacteria, and by laser ablation experiments in Figure 8C-D showing loss of feeding response when ADF is ablated.

claim: ADF neurons increase serotonin release in response to familiar food.
source: We found that recognition of familiar food activates the pair of ADF chemosensory neurons, which subsequently increase serotonin release.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 11D showing increased serotonin-positive cells on familiar food, and by genetic rescue experiments in Figure 8A showing that restoring serotonin synthesis in ADF rescues feeding behavior.

claim: Released serotonin activates the feeding response mainly by acting humorally.
source: The released serotonin activates the feeding response mainly by acting humorally and directly activates SER-7, a type 7 serotonin receptor, in MC motor neurons in the feeding organ.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that serotonin from extrapharyngeal ADF neurons activates pharyngeal MC neurons, indicating endocrine rather than synaptic signaling, as discussed in the text and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Serotonin directly activates SER-7, a type 7 serotonin receptor, in MC motor neurons in the feeding organ.
source: The released serotonin activates the feeding response mainly by acting humorally and directly activates SER-7, a type 7 serotonin receptor, in MC motor neurons in the feeding organ.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments in Figure 8E-F showing that expression of SER-7 in MC neurons rescues feeding response, and by eat-2 mutation experiments showing that blocking MC transmission suppresses the rescue effect.

claim: Worms sense the taste and/or smell of novel bacteria, which overrides the stimulatory effect of familiar bacteria on feeding by suppressing the activity of ADF or its upstream neurons.
source: Our data suggest that worms sense the taste and/or smell of novel bacteria, which overrides the stimulatory effect of familiar bacteria on feeding by suppressing the activity of ADF or its upstream neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments in Figure 14 showing that conditioned media from novel bacteria suppress feeding on familiar bacteria, and by calcium imaging in Figure 12 showing that ADF is not activated by novel bacteria.

claim: The memory of familiar food lasts for at least 7 hours in C. elegans.
source: C. elegans. The memory of familiar food lasts for at least 7 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 1D-E and 2B-E showing differential feeding rates on familiar vs novel bacteria after a 7-8 hour starvation interval.

claim: Wild-type worms feed more actively on familiar food than novel food.
source: Wild-type worms feed more actively on familiar food than novel food.
evidence: This claim is supported by feeding rate measurements presented in Figures 1, 2, 3, 7, and 10 showing consistently higher feeding rates on familiar bacteria compared to novel bacteria.

claim: Familiarity of food does not alter the feeding rates in tph-1(mg280) mutants.
source: (A)–(B) Familiarity of food does not alter the feeding rates in tph-1(mg280).
evidence: This claim is supported by feeding rate data in Figure 4A-B and Figure 5 showing no significant difference between familiar and novel food conditions in tph-1 mutants lacking serotonin synthesis.

claim: Exogenous serotonin treatment selectively increases feeding rates of wild type worms on novel food to the level of the worms on familiar food.
source: (C)–(D) Exogenous serotonin treatment selectively increases feeding rates of wild type worms on novel food to the level of the worms on familiar food.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C-D showing that serotonin treatment increases feeding rates on novel food but not on familiar food, bringing novel food feeding rates to familiar food levels.

claim: ser-7(tm1325) is defective in increasing feeding response to familiar food compared to novel food.
source: (E)–(F) ser-7(tm1325) is defective in increasing feeding response to familiar food compared to novel food.
evidence: This claim is supported by feeding rate data in Figures 4E-F and 7A-D showing that ser-7 mutants do not show the increased feeding response to familiar food that wild-type animals display.

claim: Familiarity of food does not alter the feeding rates in ser-4(ok512); mod-1(ok103); ser-7(tm1325) triple mutants.
source: Familiarity of food does not alter the feeding rates in ser-4(ok512); mod-1(ok103); ser-7(tm1325).
evidence: This claim is supported by feeding rate data in Figures 4E-F and 7C-D showing no significant difference in feeding rates between familiar and novel food in the triple mutant.

claim: Serotonin controls feeding positively via SER-7 and negatively via SER-4 and MOD-1.
source: (G) Serotonin controls feeding positively via SER-7 and negatively via SER-4 and MOD-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by feeding rate data in Figure 4G showing differential responses to serotonin in various receptor mutants, and by the model presented in Figure 7E.

claim: The feeding rate of the ser-4; mod-1; ser-7 triple null mutant is not altered by serotonin treatment.
source: The feeding rate of the ser-4; mod-1; ser-7 triple null mutant is not altered by serotonin treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4G showing no significant change in feeding rate with serotonin treatment in the triple mutant.

claim: Serotonin signaling via SER-7 that activates the feeding response is more active on familiar food than novel food.
source: (H) Serotonin signaling via SER-7 that activates the feeding response is more active on familiar food than novel food.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis in Figure 4H showing greater differences in feeding rates between wild-type and ser-7 mutants on familiar food compared to novel food, calculated from data in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Among five serotonin receptor null mutants, only ser-7(tm1325) failed to activate feeding in response to serotonin.
source: Among five serotonin receptor null mutants, only ser-7(tm1325) failed to activate feeding in response to serotonin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing feeding rates of different serotonin receptor mutants in response to serotonin treatment.

claim: A null mutation in ser-4 decreased the feeding rate in presence of serotonin but the effect was relatively small.
source: A null mutation in ser-4 also decreased the feeding rate in presence of serotonin but the effect was relatively small.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing a modest decrease in feeding rate in ser-4 mutants compared to wild-type in response to serotonin.

claim: tph-1 expression in ADF, but not in NSM, restores feeding rate in the tph-1 null mutant.
source: (A–B) tph-1 expression in ADF, but not in NSM, restores feeding rate in the tph-1 null mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments in Figure 8A-B showing that ADF-specific expression of tph-1 rescues feeding rates while NSM-specific expression does not.

claim: The rescue effect of tph-1 expression in ADF is suppressed by loss of ser-7, but not by loss of mod-5.
source: The rescue effect is suppressed by loss of ser-7, but not by loss of mod-5.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 8A showing that ser-7 mutation suppresses the ADF::tph-1 rescue effect while mod-5 mutation does not.

claim: No difference was found in feeding rates between the tph-1 single null mutant, the ser-7 single null mutant and the tph-1; ser-7 double null mutant.
source: No difference was found in feeding rates between the tph-1 single null mutant, the ser-7 single null mutant and the tph-1; ser-7 double null mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by feeding rate data in Figure 8A showing statistically indistinguishable feeding rates among these three genotypes.

claim: ADF-minus animals, but not NSM-minus animals, feed significantly less in response to familiar food.
source: (C–D) ADF-minus animals, but not NSM-minus animals, feed significantly less in response to familiar food.
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experiments in Figure 8C-D showing reduced feeding rates in ADF-ablated animals but not in NSM-ablated animals.

claim: Expression of ser-7 cDNA driven either by the flp-2 promoter or by the flp-21 promoter (MC, M4, and other neurons) but not by the ser-7b promoter (M4 only) fully restored the feeding rate in the ser-7 null mutant in response to serotonin.
source: (E) Expression of ser-7 cDNA driven either by the flp-2 promoter or by the flp-21 promoter (MC, M4, and other neurons) but not by the ser-7b promoter (M4 only) fully restored the feeding rate in the ser-7 null mutant in response to serotonin.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments in Figure 8E showing differential rescue effects with different promoters driving ser-7 expression.

claim: The rescue effect of ser-7 expression was suppressed by blocking cholinergic transmission from MC to the pharyngeal muscles.
source: The rescue effect was suppressed by blocking cholinergic transmission from MC to the pharyngeal muscles.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 8E showing that eat-2 mutation suppresses the rescue effect of pflp-21::ser-7.

claim: Expression of ser-7 cDNA driven either by the flp-2 promoter or by the flp-21 promoter fully restored the feeding rate in the ser-7 null mutant in response to familiar food.
source: (F) Expression of ser-7 cDNA driven either by the flp-2 promoter or by the flp-21 promoter fully restored the feeding rate in the ser-7 null mutant in response to familiar food.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments in Figure 8F showing that both promoters restore feeding response to familiar food in ser-7 mutants.

claim: Expression of ser-7 cDNA in M4 (and occasionally in M2) driven by the ser-7b promoter increased the feeding rate, but the effect was relatively small.
source: Expression of ser-7 cDNA in M4 (and occasionally in M2) driven by the ser-7b promoter also increased the feeding rate, but the effect was relatively small.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue data in Figure 8F showing a modest increase in feeding rate with ser-7b promoter-driven expression.

claim: ADF is more active on familiar bacteria than novel bacteria as measured by calcium imaging.
source: We tested the hypothesis first by asking if ADF is more active on familiar bacteria than novel bacteria by directly measuring the response of the ADF neurons to novel and familiar bacteria using ratiometric calcium imaging.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 12 showing greater calcium transients in ADF neurons in response to familiar bacteria compared to novel bacteria.

claim: The increase in the number of serotonin positive serotonin-uptaking cells during the 1 hr incubation on familiar food was greater than the increase on novel food.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the increase in the number of serotonin positive serotonin-uptaking cells during the 1 hr incubation on familiar food was greater than the increase on novel food (Figure 11D
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 11D showing quantification of serotonin-positive cells under different food conditions.

claim: Conditioned media from novel bacteria override the stimulatory effect of familiar bacteria on feeding.
source: (B–C) Conditioned media from novel bacteria override the stimulatory effect of familiar bacteria on feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 14B-C showing that adding conditioned media from novel bacteria to familiar bacteria reduces feeding rates to levels similar to novel food alone.

claim: Serotonin is detected in five types of neurons in C. elegans: NSM, ADF, HSN, AIM, and RIH.
source: Serotonin is detected in five types of neurons in
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans neuroanatomy, referenced in the context of the study.

claim: MC is essential for normal fast feeding on bacteria.
source: Among the pharyngeal neurons, MC is particularly interesting because it is essential for normal fast feeding on bacteria (Avery and Horvitz, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Avery and Horvitz, 1989.

claim: SER-7 was suggested to activate MC neurons.
source: SER-7 was suggested to activate MC (Hobson et al., 2006; Song and Avery, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: eat-2 encodes a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit specifically localized in the pharyngeal muscles postsynaptic to MC.
source: eat-2 encodes a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit specifically localized in the pharyngeal muscles postsynaptic to MC (McKay et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McKay et al., 2004.

claim: An eat-2 null mutation selectively blocks cholinergic transmission from MC to the pharyngeal muscles.
source: Thus, an eat-2 null mutation selectively blocks cholinergic transmission from MC to the pharyngeal muscles.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known function of eat-2 as a receptor subunit postsynaptic to MC, combined with knowledge from the cited literature.

claim: Serotonin released from extrapharyngeal ADF increased feeding in response to familiar bacteria mainly by activating SER-7 in MC directly, which in turn activates cholinergic transmission from MC to the pharyngeal muscles.
source: In summary, we conclude that serotonin released from extrapharyngeal ADF increased feeding in response to familiar bacteria mainly by activating SER-7 in MC directly, which in turn activates cholinergic transmission from MC to the pharyngeal muscles.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including genetic rescue experiments (Figure 8), ablation studies, and pharmacological manipulations showing the pathway from ADF through serotonin and SER-7 to MC and feeding behavior.

claim: Only familiar bacteria can activate ADF, and this activation causes increased serotonin release.
source: A simple explanation is that only familiar bacteria can activate ADF, and this activation causes increased serotonin release.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 12 showing ADF activation by familiar but not novel bacteria, and by immunohistochemistry in Figure 11 showing increased serotonin uptake on familiar food.

claim: Perception of the smell and/or the taste of novel bacteria suppresses feeding activation on novel food by inhibiting the activity of ADF or its upstream neurons.
source: Our results that conditioned media from novel bacteria override the stimulatory effect of familiar bacteria and suppress the feeding response (Figure 14) and that ADF is active only on familiar bacteria (Figure 12) indicate that perception of the smell and/or the taste of novel bacteria suppresses feeding activation on novel food by inhibiting the activity of ADF or its upstream neurons (Figure 15).
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with conditioned media (Figure 14) and calcium imaging (Figure 12), combined with logical inference about the mechanism.

claim: At least two neural pathways should act antagonistically in controlling the activity of ADF or its upstream neurons.
source: Given that familiar food substantially increased ADF activity compared to the baseline (Figure 12A,B), at least two neural pathways should act antagonistically in controlling the activity of ADF or its upstream neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ADF shows increased activity on familiar food and decreased activity on novel food compared to baseline, suggesting opposing regulatory inputs.

claim: ADF or its upstream neurons are positively regulated by perception of food and negatively regulated by perception of olfactory and gustatory cues of novel bacteria.
source: The simplest model would be that ADF or its upstream neurons are positively regulated by perception of food and negatively regulated by perception of olfactory and gustatory cues of novel bacteria (Figure 15).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental observations of ADF activity patterns and the effects of conditioned media.

claim: C. elegans remembers two bacterial types at least for 24 hours.
source: Preliminary data show that C. elegans remembers two bacterial types at least for 24 hr (data not shown)
evidence: This claim is stated as preliminary unpublished data.

claim: Serotonin transmission from ADF is critical for the learned aversion to pathogenic bacteria.
source: Interestingly, serotonin transmission from ADF was also shown to be critical for the learned aversion to pathogenic bacteria (Zhang et al., 2005; Ha et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mere exposure to particular food alters subsequent consumption of the food in many different species.
source: Accumulated studies show that mere exposure to particular food alters subsequent consumption of the food in many different species (Pliner et al., 1993; Wang and Provenza, 1996; Diaz-Cenzano and Chotro, 2010; Morin-Audebrand et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in different species.

claim: Feeding regulation by familiarity discrimination is conserved across species.
source: suggesting that feeding regulation by familiarity discrimination is conserved across species.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that multiple species show altered food consumption after exposure, as documented in cited literature.

claim: Some species including humans consume familiar food more actively than novel food, probably to avoid possible pathogens.
source: Some species including humans consume familiar food more actively than novel food (Diaz-Cenzano and Chotro, 2010), probably to avoid possible pathogens.
evidence: This claim combines cited empirical observations with speculative reasoning about evolutionary function.

claim: Other species consume familiar food less actively than novel food, probably to assure balanced nutrition intake.
source: In contrast, other species consume familiar food less actively than novel food (Wang and Provenza, 1996), probably to assure balanced nutrition intake.
evidence: This claim combines cited empirical observations with speculative reasoning about evolutionary function.

claim: The nervous system in C. elegans senses various aspects of food, such as the efficiency with which it supports growth and its pathogenicity, and triggers behavioral plasticity.
source: The nervous system in C. elegans senses various aspects of food, such as the efficiency with which it supports growth (Shtonda and Avery, 2006) and its pathogenicity (Zhang et al., 2005), and triggers behavioral plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: The nervous system in C. elegans can form memories of various olfactory or gustatory cues.
source: The nervous system can also form memories of various olfactory or gustatory cues (Bargmann, 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Prior exposure to particular bacteria selectively increases feeding in response to those bacteria.
source: We first showed that regulation of feeding by familiarity discrimination is conserved in C. elegans by showing that (1) Prior exposure to particular bacteria selectively increases feeding in response to those bacteria
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 1-3 showing differential feeding rates based on prior exposure.

claim: The behavior of increased feeding on familiar bacteria depends on the duration of exposure, but not on the timing of exposure or nutritional status.
source: (2) The behavior depends on the duration of exposure, but not on the timing of exposure (Figure 3) or nutritional status (Figure 1B–E)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing duration dependence and Figures 1B-E showing independence from nutritional status.

claim: C. elegans retains the memory of familiar bacteria for at least 7 hours.
source: (3) C. elegans retains the memory of familiar bacteria for at least 7 hr (Figure 1D,E and 2B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential feeding responses after 7-8 hour intervals.

claim: The C. elegans nervous system may have evolved to increase the probability of consuming wholesome food by using past food experiences as in higher vertebrates and humans.
source: We speculate that the C. elegans nervous system may have evolved this way to increase the probability of consuming wholesome food by using past food experiences as in higher vertebrates and humans.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation about evolutionary function.

claim: Naïve worms are attracted to the smell of pathogenic bacteria but develop aversion to it after experience.
source: It was previously shown that naïve worms are attracted to the smell of pathogenic bacteria but develop aversion to it after experience (Zhang et al., 2005; Ha et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pathogenic bacteria kill worms in 4 hours.
source: The pathogenic bacteria kill worms in 4 hr (Zhang et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: It would be detrimental for worms to increase consumption of pathogenic bacteria.
source: and thus, it would be detrimental for worms to increase consumption of the bacteria.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known lethality of pathogenic bacteria.

claim: Given that NSM is a prominent reservoir of serotonin in the pharynx, and that NSM is implicated in regulating the enhanced slowing response on food, it is surprising that serotonin in NSM does not affect feeding in presence of familiar food.
source: Given that NSM is a prominent reservoir of serotonin in the pharynx, and that NSM is implicated in regulating the enhanced slowing response on food (Sawin et al., 2000), it is surprising that serotonin in NSM does not affect feeding in presence of familiar food.
evidence: This combines established knowledge from cited literature with the surprising experimental finding from Figure 8.

claim: NSM releases little or no serotonin, which is insufficient to activate MC neurons in the pharynx in response to familiar food.
source: One plausible explanation is that NSM releases little or no serotonin, which is insufficient to activate MC neurons in the pharynx in response to familiar food.
evidence: This is proposed as a speculative explanation for the experimental observation.

claim: Serotonin from NSM has only a small effect on the enhanced slowing response.
source: This explanation does not contradict previously reported NSM function in the enhanced slowing response (Sawin et al., 2000) because serotonin from NSM has only a small effect on the behavior (Sawin et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An endocrine serotonin signal from ADF, not a local serotonin signal from NSM, may have been employed for the feeding activation on familiar food to systemically control multiple behaviors and physiological adaptations.
source: An endocrine serotonin signal from ADF, not a local serotonin signal from NSM, may have been employed for the feeding activation on familiar food to systemically control multiple behaviors and physiological adaptations.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional significance of using ADF rather than NSM.

claim: The feeding rates on HB101 were significantly higher than the rate on DA1878 in non-starved wild-type worms (p=0.006).
source: since the feeding rates on HB101 were significantly higher than the rate on DA1878 (in non-starved wild-type worms [p=0.006]
evidence: This is a statistical result from experimental data comparing feeding rates on different bacteria.

claim: The feeding rates on HB101 were significantly higher than the rate on DA1878 in 7-8 hr starved wild-type worms (p=0.003).
source: and in 7–8 hr starved wild-type worms [p=0.003])
evidence: This is a statistical result from experimental data comparing feeding rates on different bacteria.

claim: The feeding rate on HB101 was significantly higher than the rate on JU54 (p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from experimental data comparing feeding rates on different bacteria.

claim: The feeding rate on PA14 pstP was significantly higher than the rate on HB101 (p=0.001).
source: and since the feeding rate on PA14 pstP was significantly higher than the rate on HB101 (p=0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from experimental data comparing feeding rates on different bacteria.

claim: Like wild type worms, ser-4(ok512); mod-1(ok103) show increased feeding response on familiar food compared to novel food.
source: Like wild type worms, ser-4(ok512); mod-1(ok103) show increased feeding response on familiar food compared to novel food.
evidence: This claim is supported by feeding rate data in Figure 9 showing differential responses to familiar vs novel food in the double mutant.

claim: Wild-type male worms show increased feeding response on familiar food compared to novel food.
source: Feeding rates of wild-type male worms on HB101 (A) and DA1878 (B) after a 7- to 8-hr interval from training the animals on one or the other bacterium.
evidence: This claim is supported by feeding rate data in Figure 10 showing differential responses in male worms, though the text does not explicitly state the conclusion.

claim: SER-7 is expressed mostly in pharyngeal neurons.
source: SER-7 is expressed mostly in pharyngeal neurons (Hobson et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Pharyngeal neurons regulate the motions of pharyngeal muscles.
source: which regulate the motions of pharyngeal muscles (Avery and Horvitz, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and represents established knowledge.

claim: The flp-21 and the flp-2 promoters drive expression in several neurons, and the expression patterns of the two promoters overlap only in MC and M4.
source: The flp-21 and the flp-2 promoters drive expression in several neurons, and the expression patterns of the two promoters overlap only in MC and M4 (Kim and Li, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study characterizing these promoters.

claim: Both pflp-21::SER-7 and pflp-2::SER-7 fully rescued the feeding rate in the ser-7 mutant in response to familiar food as well as serotonin.
source: We found that both pflp-21::SER-7 and pflp-2::SER-7 fully rescued the feeding rate in the ser-7 mutant in response to familiar food as well as serotonin (Figure 8E,F
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue data in Figures 8E and 8F.

claim: Expression of SER-7 in M4 and occasionally in M2 using the ser-7b promoter failed to alter the pumping rate and had only a small effect on pumping in the ser-7 null mutant in response to serotonin and familiar food, respectively.
source: In contrast, expression of SER-7 in M4 and occasionally in M2 using the ser-7b promoter failed to alter the pumping rate and had only a small effect on pumping in the ser-7 null mutant in response to serotonin and familiar food, respectively (Figure 8E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic rescue data in Figures 8E and 8F showing limited rescue with the ser-7b promoter.

claim: SER-7 in MC activates pharyngeal pumping.
source: suggesting that SER-7 in MC activates pharyngeal pumping.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of rescue effects with different promoters that overlap only in MC.

claim: The failure of rescue with ser-7b promoter is unlikely to be due to insufficient expression because expression of the rescue construct significantly activated isthmus peristalsis, the other feeding motion in C. elegans, which is controlled by M4.
source: The failure of rescue is unlikely to be due to insufficient expression because expression of the rescue construct significantly activated isthmus peristalsis, the other feeding motion in C. elegans, which is controlled by M4 (Song and Avery, 2012).
evidence: This claim combines experimental observation with citation to support an inference about expression levels.

claim: The eat-2 null mutation suppressed the rescue effect of pflp-21::ser-7(+) in response to serotonin.
source: We found that the eat-2 null mutation suppressed the rescue effect of pflp-21::ser-7(+) in response to serotonin (Figure 8E)
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 8E.

claim: Pharyngeal pumping rate was lower in the eat-2; ser-7 double null mutant than the eat-2 single null mutant (p<0.001).
source: #Pharyngeal pumping rate was lower in the eat-2; ser-7 double null mutant than the eat-2 single null mutant (p<0.001)

claim: Pharyngeal pumping rate was lower in the eat-2; ser-7 double null mutant than the ser-7 single null mutant (p=0.002).
source: and the ser-7 single null mutant (p=0.002).

claim: Acetylcholine marginally activates pumping in an EAT-2-independent manner and there is residual acetylcholine release in absence of SER-7 in response to serotonin.
source: The difference suggests that acetylcholine marginally activates pumping in an EAT-2-independent manner and that there is residual acetylcholine release in absence of SER-7 in response to serotonin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed differences in pumping rates between mutants.

claim: No difference in feeding rates was found between the eat-2; ser-7 mutant expressing pflp-21::gfp and the mutant expressing pflp-21::ser-7 cDNA.
source: No difference in feeding rates was found between the eat-2; ser-7 mutant expressing pflp-21::gfp and the mutant expressing pflp-21::ser-7 cDNA.
evidence: This is a statistical result from experimental data in Figure 8E showing no rescue effect when MC transmission is blocked.

claim: Like the positive SER-7-mediated signal, the inhibitory SER-4- and MOD-1-mediated serotonin signaling is more active on familiar food than novel food, but it decreases the feeding rate.
source: Like the positive SER-7-mediated signal, the inhibitory SER-4- and MOD-1-mediated serotonin signaling is more active on familiar food than novel food, but it decreases the feeding rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis in Figure 7F showing greater inhibitory effects on familiar food.

claim: Serotonin signaling via SER-4 and MOD-1 that suppresses the feeding response on familiar food is more active on HB101 than DA1878.
source: (F) Serotonin signaling via SER-4 and MOD-1 that suppresses the feeding response on familiar food is more active on HB101 than DA1878.

claim: On novel food the feeding rate of wild-type is slightly higher than that of the ser-7 null mutant.
source: On novel food the feeding rate of wild-type is slightly higher than that of the ser-7 null mutant.

claim: The difference in feeding rates between wild-type and ser-7 mutant on novel food may be due to constitutive activity of SER-7; that is, SER-7 is active to some extent even in absence of its ligand, serotonin.
source: The difference may be due to constitutive activity of SER-7; that is, SER-7 is active to some extent even in absence of its ligand, serotonin (Hobson et al., 2003).

source: (A–B). No serotonin signal was detected in the tph-1(mg280);Is[ptph-1::gfp] (A) and in the mod-5(n3314);tph-1(mg280);Is[ptph-1::gfp] (B) mutant animals.

source: (A–B). No serotonin signal was detected in the tph-1(mg280);Is[ptph-1::gfp] (A) and in the mod-5(n3314);tph-1(mg280);Is[ptph-1::gfp] (B) mutant animals.
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemistry data in Figure 13.

claim: In DA2300, serotonin signal was found in four different classes of serotonergic neurons (ADF, NSM, RIH and AIM).
source: In DA2300, serotonin signal was found in four different classes of serotonergic neurons (ADF, NSM, RIH and AIM).
